title: The four pillars of OOP
scopeHtml: Scope: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism, each tied to a real design decision, with JVM dispatch and vtable depth. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: The four pillars at a glance
notes.html:
Encapsulation hides data behind rules, abstraction hides complexity behind a simple contract, inheritance reuses a parent's code, polymorphism lets one call do different things depending on the real object. Interviewers do not want the definitions; they want to hear what design decision each pillar buys you and what it costs.

Pillar Real decision Cost if misused
Encapsulation Keep invariants in one class Getter/setter bags give false safety
Abstraction Callers depend on an interface Leaky or premature abstractions
Inheritance Share state/code in a true "is-a" Fragile base class, tight coupling
Polymorphism Replace if/else with dispatch Hard-to-trace call paths

Worked example. A payments module with 4 methods (card, UPI, wallet, netbanking) and 12 if (type == ...) branches in 5 places has 60 places to forget when you add method 5. Pillars 2 and 4 collapse that to 1 new class.

Industry examples. Android View hierarchy (inheritance + polymorphic onDraw), JDBC (abstraction), Java String (encapsulation: immutable, internals can change from char[] to byte[], which happened in Java 9 with compact strings, without breaking callers).

Everyday analogy. A car: the dashboard is the abstraction, the sealed engine bay is encapsulation, "all cars have wheels and an engine" is inheritance, and pressing the accelerator works the same on petrol or electric (polymorphism).

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting definitions with no example from a system you built.
  • Presenting inheritance as the main tool; modern advice is composition first (see the design principles note).

notes.title: Encapsulation: guard the invariant
notes.html:
Encapsulation means an object owns its data and is the only one allowed to change it, so its rules can never be broken from outside. An invariant is a rule that must always be true, such as "balance never below zero" or "end date is after start date".

Mechanism: private fields plus methods that validate. In Java, access is enforced by the compiler and the JVM at link time; reflection can still break in (setAccessible), and since Java 9 modules (JPMS) and since 16/17 strong encapsulation of JDK internals make that harder.

Before (anyone can break the rule):

class Account { public long balance; }
acc.balance -= 5000;          // overdraft, no audit, no thread safety

After (rule enforced in one place, thread-safe):

final class Account {
    private long balance;                          // cents
    synchronized void withdraw(long cents) {
        if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount");
        if (cents > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
        balance -= cents;
    }
    synchronized long balance() { return balance; }
}
class Account {
    var balance = 0L; private set
    @Synchronized fun withdraw(cents: Long) {
        require(cents > 0); check(cents <= balance) { "insufficient funds" }
        balance -= cents
    }
}

Worked example. Two threads each withdraw 700 from a balance of 1000 with an unsynchronised check-then-act: both pass the check (700 <= 1000), both subtract, balance becomes -400. With the lock, the second sees 300 and fails. Real banks do this in the database (UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - 700 WHERE id = ? AND balance >= 700, check rows updated = 1).

  caller --> [ withdraw() ] --guards--> [ private balance ]
  caller -X-----------------------------> direct access blocked

Industry examples. Java's String, BigDecimal and LocalDate are immutable so they can never be left half-changed. Kotlin private set and Android ViewModel exposing StateFlow (read-only) while keeping MutableStateFlow private is the same pattern.

Everyday analogy. An ATM: you cannot reach into the vault, you can only press buttons that follow the bank's rules.

Decision gravity. Private fields with behaviour methods are reversible and cheap now. A public mutable field or a getter that returns the internal List is a one-way door; callers will mutate it. Return List.copyOf(items) or Collections.unmodifiableList(items).

Common interview traps.

  • A getter returning a mutable collection or Date leaks the internals.
  • Auto-generated getters and setters for every field are not encapsulation.
  • Forgetting that encapsulation also covers concurrency: invariants across two fields need one lock.

notes.title: Abstraction: hide the how
notes.html:
Abstraction means showing only what the caller needs and hiding the rest. Encapsulation is about protecting data; abstraction is about simplifying what you present.

Mechanism: interfaces and abstract classes define a vocabulary (send(message)), and implementations hide transport, retries, auth and format. Good abstractions are stable while implementations change.

Before (caller knows SMTP, SMS and push details):

void notifyUser(User u, String text) {
    if (u.prefersEmail) { Properties p = new Properties(); /* 20 lines of SMTP */ }
    else if (u.prefersSms) { /* HTTP to the SMS vendor */ }
}

After:

interface Notifier { void send(String userId, String text); }

class EmailNotifier implements Notifier { public void send(String u, String t) { /* SMTP hidden */ } }
class SmsNotifier   implements Notifier { public void send(String u, String t) { /* vendor HTTP hidden */ } }

class OrderService {
    private final Notifier notifier;
    OrderService(Notifier n) { this.notifier = n; }
    void shipped(String userId) { notifier.send(userId, "Your order shipped"); }
}
fun interface Notifier { fun send(userId: String, text: String) }
class OrderService(private val notifier: Notifier) { fun shipped(userId: String) = notifier.send(userId, "Your order shipped") }

Worked example. Swapping the SMS vendor (vendor A at Rs 0.18/SMS to vendor B at Rs 0.12/SMS) changes one class. At 5M SMS a month that is Rs 300,000 saved, and OrderService is untouched.

Industry examples. JDBC and Android Room hide the database; Retrofit hides HTTP; Kafka producer API hides partitioning and batching. Netflix's Hystrix/Resilience4j wrap calls behind a stable surface.

Everyday analogy. Driving: steering wheel and pedals, not fuel injection timing.

Decision gravity. Abstract at a point of real change (vendors, storage, platforms), not everywhere. A wrong abstraction is worse than duplication: callers shape themselves around it and it becomes a one-way door once public. The "rule of three": wait for the third use before extracting.

Common interview traps.

  • Leaky abstraction: an InMemoryStore interface that exposes flushToDisk().
  • Abstract class vs interface: abstract class carries state and partial code; interface is a contract, and a class can have many.
  • Confusing abstraction (design idea) with the abstract keyword (one tool).

notes.title: Inheritance: reuse with a catch
notes.html:
Inheritance lets a child class get the parent's fields and methods and override some. It models "is-a": a SavingsAccount is an Account.

Mechanism: a child object in memory holds the parent's fields first, then its own, so a child reference can be treated as the parent type (upcast). super(...) runs the parent constructor first. Java has single class inheritance only, to avoid the diamond problem on state; default methods bring limited multiple inheritance of behaviour.

Before (copy-paste):

class CurrentAccount { long bal; void deposit(long c){ bal += c; } void withdraw(long c){ /* 10 lines */ } }
class SavingsAccount { long bal; void deposit(long c){ bal += c; } void withdraw(long c){ /* same 10 lines */ } }

After (genuine is-a, shared code once):

abstract class Account {
    protected long balance;
    void deposit(long c) { balance += c; }
    void withdraw(long c) { if (c > limit()) throw new IllegalStateException(); balance -= c; }
    protected abstract long limit();
}
class Savings extends Account { protected long limit() { return balance; } }
class Current extends Account { protected long limit() { return balance + 50_000; } } // overdraft
abstract class Account(protected var balance: Long = 0) {
    fun deposit(c: Long) { balance += c }
    fun withdraw(c: Long) { check(c <= limit()); balance -= c }
    protected abstract fun limit(): Long
}
class Savings : Account() { override fun limit() = balance }
class Current : Account() { override fun limit() = balance + 50_000 }
        +-----------------+
        |  Account        |
        |  #balance       |
        |  +deposit()     |
        |  +withdraw()    |
        |  #limit()  {abs}|
        +--------^--------+
          +------+------+
   +------+-----+  +----+-------+
   |  Savings   |  |  Current   |
   +------------+  +------------+

Worked example (the catch). Classic Liskov violation: Square extends Rectangle with setWidth also setting height. Code that does r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); area == 20 fails for a Square (gives 16). Inheritance promises a child can stand in for the parent everywhere; if it cannot, it is wrong.

Industry examples. Android AppCompatActivity extends FragmentActivity ... is a deep chain that makes behaviour hard to follow; Google moved towards composition (Jetpack ViewModel, Lifecycle observers). Java's Stack extends Vector is a famous mistake: it exposes insertElementAt, breaking stack discipline. Effective Java: "Design and document for inheritance or else prohibit it" (hence final classes).

Everyday analogy. A family recipe: the child recipe starts as the parent's and tweaks one ingredient; but if you change the parent recipe, every child dish changes too.

Decision gravity. Inheritance is the tightest coupling Java offers; changing a parent can silently break every child (fragile base class). Choose it only for a stable, true is-a with substitutability; prefer composition otherwise. Moving from inheritance to composition later means rewriting every subclass: a one-way door in practice.

Common interview traps.

  • Inheriting just to reuse code when the relationship is "has-a" or "uses-a".
  • Overriding a method that the parent calls inside its own code (self-use) without knowing it.
  • protected fields: they are part of the public API to every subclass, ever.

notes.title: Polymorphism: one call, many behaviours
notes.html:
Polymorphism means the same method call runs different code depending on the real type of the object. shape.area() works for circles and squares without the caller checking which.

Two kinds. Compile-time (overloading): the compiler picks the method from the declared argument types. Runtime (overriding): the JVM picks from the actual object type when the code runs. Interviews usually mean the second.

Before (type-checking by hand):

double area(Object s) {
    if (s instanceof Circle c) return Math.PI * c.r * c.r;
    if (s instanceof Rect r) return r.w * r.h;
    throw new IllegalArgumentException();       // new shape = edit this method
}

After:

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rect { double area(); }
record Circle(double r) implements Shape { public double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; } }
record Rect(double w, double h) implements Shape { public double area() { return w * h; } }

double total = shapes.stream().mapToDouble(Shape::area).sum();
sealed interface Shape { fun area(): Double }
data class Circle(val r: Double) : Shape { override fun area() = Math.PI * r * r }
data class Rect(val w: Double, val h: Double) : Shape { override fun area() = w * h }

Worked example. Circle(2) gives about 12.57, Rect(3,4) gives 12. A list of 1,000 mixed shapes is summed in one loop with zero instanceof. Adding Triangle is one new record; the compiler flags exhaustive switch sites for sealed types.

Industry examples. Spring injects different PaymentGateway beans per profile; java.util.List lets you swap ArrayList for LinkedList; Android's RecyclerView.Adapter and Compose's @Composable slots rely on it.

Everyday analogy. Saying "dance" to a crowd: ballet dancers, breakdancers and your uncle each do it their own way.

Decision gravity. Polymorphism is open for new types but closed for new operations (adding perimeter() touches all classes); switch over a sealed type is the reverse. This is the expression problem. Pick polymorphism when types grow, pattern-matching switch when operations grow.

Common interview traps.

  • Overloading is resolved at compile time on the declared type: print(Object o) vs print(String s) with Object x = "hi"; print(x) calls the Object version.
  • Fields and static methods are not polymorphic (they are hidden, not overridden).
  • Overriding with a weaker access modifier or a broader checked exception is illegal.

notes.title: JVM dispatch and the vtable
notes.html:
Under the hood, a virtual call is a lookup in a per-class table of method addresses. Knowing this lets you explain why polymorphism is cheap and when it is not.

Mechanism. Each class has a vtable (virtual method table) in its metadata (HotSpot: Klass). Every instance has an object header with a pointer to its class (the "klass word", 4 bytes with compressed class pointers). A child's vtable starts as a copy of the parent's, and overridden slots are replaced with the child's method; new methods are appended. A call shape.area() compiles to invokevirtual Shape.area; at runtime the VM loads the object's class, reads the vtable slot (a fixed index known at link time), and jumps. Interface calls (invokeinterface) cannot use one fixed index because a class implements many interfaces, so they use an itable search or cached lookup, which is a bit slower when cold.

 Circle object                 Circle.class vtable
 +-----------+                 slot0 toString -> Object.toString
 | header    |--klass-------->  slot1 equals   -> Object.equals
 | r = 2.0   |                 slot2 area     -> Circle.area   <== overridden
 +-----------+                 slot3 perimeter-> Circle.perimeter

What the JIT does. The HotSpot C2 compiler profiles each call site. If it has only ever seen one class (monomorphic) it inlines the method behind a cheap class-check guard, so the call costs about the same as a plain call or less. With two types (bimorphic) it still inlines both with checks. With three or more (megamorphic) it falls back to a real vtable or itable call, roughly a few nanoseconds extra and, more important, it blocks inlining, which blocks later optimisations. Class Hierarchy Analysis also lets it devirtualise a method when only one loaded class overrides it, and deoptimise if a new class loads later. final methods and classes help the compiler, though the JIT often figures it out anyway.

Worked example. A hot loop doing 100M shape.area() calls on one type: JIT inlines, about 0.3 ns/call, roughly 30 ms in total. The same loop over a random mix of 5 types: megamorphic, about 3 to 5 ns/call, roughly 300 to 500 ms. Treat these as order of magnitude; always measure with JMH. In normal business code (network and DB at 1 to 50 ms) this difference is irrelevant; it matters in tight numeric or serialisation loops.

Overload vs override at bytecode level. The overload is chosen by javac and written into the bytecode as a specific method descriptor; the override is chosen at runtime by the vtable. invokestatic, invokespecial (constructors, super.x(), private methods) and invokevirtual are different instructions; invokedynamic powers lambdas and string concatenation.

Industry examples. The Netty and Kafka code bases avoid megamorphic hot paths (a few concrete handler types per call site). The Truffle/Graal and JMH docs discuss type profile pollution, and Java's own Collections code keeps sort comparators cheap this way.

Everyday analogy. A phone book with fixed page numbers per name: the receptionist looks at who you are (header), flips to the fixed page (slot) and dials the number (method).

Decision gravity. Do not hand-optimise away polymorphism for speed; readability wins and the JIT is good. Only restructure a measured hot path (for example, group items by type before looping). This is reversible and local.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "virtual calls are slow"; mostly false after JIT inlining. The honest answer is monomorphic/bimorphic calls are cheap, megamorphic ones are not.
  • Calling an overridable method from a constructor (dispatch uses the real class, but its fields are not yet initialised).
  • Kotlin classes are final by default; you must write open. Java is open by default. Kotlin's override keyword is mandatory.

notes.title: Tying the pillars to a real design
notes.html:
Take one feature, "send a receipt", and use all four pillars on purpose.

  <<interface>> ReceiptChannel        (abstraction)
        ^                 ^
  EmailReceipt        SmsReceipt      (polymorphism: both used via the interface)
        ^
  HtmlEmailReceipt                    (inheritance: only for a true specialisation)

  Receipt { private lines; total() }  (encapsulation: totals computed inside)
final class Receipt {
    private final List<Long> lineCents;
    Receipt(List<Long> l) { this.lineCents = List.copyOf(l); }       // encapsulated + immutable
    long total() { return lineCents.stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum(); }
}
interface ReceiptChannel { void deliver(String to, Receipt r); }     // abstraction
class EmailReceipt implements ReceiptChannel { public void deliver(String to, Receipt r) { /* SMTP */ } }
class SmsReceipt   implements ReceiptChannel { public void deliver(String to, Receipt r) { /* SMS */ } }

class ReceiptService {
    private final List<ReceiptChannel> channels;                      // polymorphism at work
    ReceiptService(List<ReceiptChannel> c) { channels = c; }
    void send(String to, Receipt r) { channels.forEach(ch -> ch.deliver(to, r)); }
}
class Receipt(lines: List<Long>) { private val lineCents = lines.toList(); fun total() = lineCents.sum() }
interface ReceiptChannel { fun deliver(to: String, r: Receipt) }
class ReceiptService(private val channels: List<ReceiptChannel>) {
    fun send(to: String, r: Receipt) = channels.forEach { it.deliver(to, r) }
}

Worked example. Adding WhatsApp receipts (WhatsApp Business API) is 1 new class implementing ReceiptChannel, 0 edits to ReceiptService, plus a test with a fake channel. Cost: 1 afternoon vs 2 days of finding every if (channel == ...).

Industry examples. Uber and Swiggy notification services use a channel interface with push, SMS, email and WhatsApp implementations selected by user preference and cost.

Everyday analogy. A postal service: one "deliver this" contract, many trucks and couriers, and the letter itself sealed in an envelope.

Common interview traps.

  • Naming all four pillars but being unable to show one concrete decision for each.
  • Using inheritance for HtmlEmailReceipt when a format strategy field would do.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Encapsulation guards invariants in one place (private state, validated methods, no leaked mutable internals, locks for concurrent invariants).
  • Abstraction hides the how behind a stable contract; put it at real points of change, wait for the rule of three.
  • Inheritance is for stable, substitutable is-a only; it is the tightest coupling and a one-way door; prefer composition.
  • Polymorphism replaces type-checking with dispatch: open for new types, closed for new operations (expression problem; sealed + switch is the opposite trade).
  • JVM: invokevirtual uses a vtable slot from the object's klass pointer; invokeinterface uses itable lookup; JIT inlines mono/bimorphic sites and slows at megamorphic ones.
  • Overloading is compile-time, overriding is runtime; fields and statics are not polymorphic; never call overridable methods from constructors.
